summary: inductance (L) (Results) is what the Impedance matching calculator works out, and it gets there from the frequency, the source resistance, the source reactance and the load resistance. Think of it as a shortcut for whatever you happen to be working on. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Impedance matching calculator work?
sections.html:
The Impedance matching calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports inductance (L) (Results) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the circuit type, the circuit DC current and show plot?); then you type in the frequency (F), the source resistance (RS), the source reactance (XS) and the load resistance (RL).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the Impedance matching calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Inductance (L)=(load resistance (RL), source resistance (RS), load reactance (XL), source reactance (XS), frequency (F), circuit DC current)
Capacitance (C)=(load resistance (RL), source resistance (RS), load reactance (XL), source reactance (XS), frequency (F), circuit DC current)
Q factor=(load resistance (RL), source resistance (RS), load reactance (XL), source reactance (XS), circuit DC current)
Inductance (L)=(load resistance (RL), source resistance (RS), load reactance (XL), source reactance (XS), frequency (F), q factor)
Source capacitance (CS)=(load resistance (RL), source resistance (RS), source reactance (XS), frequency (F), q factor)
Load capacitance (CL)=(load resistance (RL), source resistance (RS), load reactance (XL), source reactance (XS), frequency (F), q factor)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Frequency, opening in megahertz
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Inductance – henry, opening in nanohenries
  • Capacitance, opening in picofarads
  • Inductance – henry, opening in nanohenries

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Impedance matching calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the frequency, the source resistance and the source reactance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Impedance matching calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns inductance (L) (Results), derived from the frequency, the source resistance and the source reactance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Impedance matching calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the frequency, the source resistance, the source reactance and the load resistance, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter frequency (F) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Frequency (F) opens in megahertz and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Impedance matching calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
